purpose: Reorder archive work by closure potential after expanding the source registry through Cambridge, Coimbra, Würzburg, Manchester, Melbourne, Jena and Dundee. Priority is based on the chance of connecting a preparation to a historical address, transaction, publication, teaching sequence, apparatus, or collection system.
rules: Do not rank by collection size, institutional prestige, or geographic novelty.
Prefer a bounded historical system with named ledgers, catalogues, trays, labels, serial sections, or maker identities.
Keep object survival and documentary survival separate: either side can remain when the other is lost.
Preserve conflicting collection counts as dated source states rather than harmonising them silently.
For teaching collections, capture the relation among preparations, instruments, course order, student use, and storage rather than counting slides alone.
For commercial/private cabinets, capture maker, subject, label, tray position, date, locality, retailer, and any historical catalogue number before interpreting ownership or exchange.

tier_S_immediate_closure.why_now: Existing Cole evidence already supplies the publication side of the crosswalk; the cheapest unresolved step is searching the Club's label transcription and cabinet documentation for surviving Cole preparations.
tier_S_immediate_closure.first_action: Search Cole / Martin J. Cole / Prize Medal / Studies and diagnostic Volume I subjects in existing label data before requesting new photography.
tier_S_immediate_closure.closure: historical subscription → cabinet entry → surviving preparation

tier_S_immediate_closure.target: Oxford History of Science Museum — RMS archive and slide cabinet
tier_S_immediate_closure.why_now: The project already has itemised RMS receipt, donation and exhibition events; Oxford preserves both the institutional archive and the large surviving RMS cabinet.
tier_S_immediate_closure.first_action: Request old slide indexes/catalogues and query two or three already itemised corpus events before broad archival work.
tier_S_immediate_closure.closure: journal event → society record → surviving slide

tier_S_immediate_closure.target: University of Tokyo Medical Library — Anatomy Department records
tier_S_immediate_closure.why_now: The archival sequence is already bounded by record numbers and dates: course diary, preparation quantity ledger, manufactured-item catalogue, microscope/instrument index and practical microscopy records.
tier_S_immediate_closure.first_action: Request page images or digitisation for nos. 110 and 118–123, preserving page order and covers/labels.
tier_S_immediate_closure.closure: manufacture/inventory → microscope/apparatus → practical use → course chronology

tier_S_immediate_closure.target: University Museum of Zoology Cambridge — Balfour/Darwin historical slide systems
tier_S_immediate_closure.why_now: The Museum explicitly preserves historical slides together with collector catalogues/notebooks and, in some cases, original cabinets. Balfour's surviving serial sections can also be paired with surviving microscopy apparatus and publication captions.
tier_S_immediate_closure.first_action: Ask for the Balfour slide-series inventory, current cabinet/box order, any original labels/catalogues, and object-level links to the Whipple Balfour apparatus.
tier_S_immediate_closure.closure: serial section → apparatus/production technique → publication → current museum address

tier_S_immediate_closure.target: Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn Historical Archives
tier_S_immediate_closure.why_now: The Naples catalogue and 1880 RMS twelve-slide shipment already close nine subjects strongly; an internal account/order/dispatch record could turn this into transaction-level history.
tier_S_immediate_closure.first_action: Search 1879–1881 copybooks, preparation-department accounts and Waters correspondence against the nine matched catalogue numbers.
tier_S_immediate_closure.closure: catalogue offering → internal transaction → RMS shipment

tier_S_immediate_closure.target: Museo de La Plata — Tempère & Peragallo / Möller
tier_S_immediate_closure.why_now: Numbered historical series survive in the same institution that preserves museum correspondence and departmental records from the 1880s onward.
tier_S_immediate_closure.first_action: Obtain current box/tray inventory and label photographs before searching archive correspondence for acquisition or exchange.
tier_S_immediate_closure.closure: series number → museum address → acquisition/exchange record

tier_S_immediate_closure.target: Whipple Museum — Charles Elcock working archive
tier_S_immediate_closure.why_now: Raw specimens, unfinished material, tools, stains, labels, finished slides and cabinets survive together.
tier_S_immediate_closure.first_action: Build an association map from accession records and object groupings before selecting representative workflows for high-resolution documentation.
tier_S_immediate_closure.closure: raw material → preparation operation → label → finished slide → cabinet/commercial object

tier_A_high_value_comparators.target: University of Coimbra — Costa Simões histology/physiology teaching system
tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: How were course content, microscopic preparations and experimental-physiology apparatus catalogued as one pedagogical system in 1873?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Parse the 1873 catalogue row by row and compare its internal categories with the course programme and surviving visual/institutional documentation. Verify whether any original preparations or apparatus survive before making object-continuity claims.

tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: Can surviving early histological sections be connected to Kölliker's microscopy teaching, methods and publications?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Request an inventory of slides attributed to Kölliker, label images, historical catalogue references, and any course/institute records that preserve original ordering or use.

tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: Can labelled private-cabinet slides be reverse-matched to nineteenth-century commercial suppliers and catalogues?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Obtain the tray-by-tray report or structured transcription. Preserve the published tray-count discrepancy: a 2023 University article describes 22 trays, while a 2024 article describes 25 numbered trays. Treat both as dated descriptions until the current inventory is checked.

tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: How did a zoology department founded in 1887 use and retain microscope slides contributed by Walter Baldwin Spencer and later researchers?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Request the historical-slide inventory by creator/date, any original departmental registers, and the relation between slide holdings, reprints and teaching records.

tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: How does one physical preparation accumulate laboratory, inventory, legacy, archival and digital addresses?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Sample a bounded set and reconstruct every identifier namespace with dates and administrative context.

tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: How can a slide label carry method, date, interpretation, publication reference and remounting history at once?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Obtain front/back images and full catalogue data for a small cholera/histology sample, then crosswalk to the 1889 manuscript catalogue.

tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: How does a sample number work across raw material, slide, catalogue, drawing and annotated book?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Sample one documented number through every surviving medium rather than starting with a global inventory.

tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: What relations are lost when one integrated scientific estate is split among libraries, botanical collections and instrument museums?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Reconstruct the 1910 acquisition and later transfers with one cross-institutional provenance table.

tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: Can named Watson & Sons and Hornell & Sinel objects be matched to catalogue/periodical series descriptions?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Capture full labels, series numbers and collection coordinates for the published examples and then search the UK corpus.

tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: How did preparations and microscopic glass slides move through gift, purchase, research loan and specimen exchange?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Run a bounded TEI keyword harvest for Präparat*, Mikroskop*, Glastäfelchen, Objektträger, Radiolar*, Ankauf, Versand and preparator names; extract sender/recipient/date/object/relation.

tier_A_high_value_comparators.question: What can and cannot be reconstructed when the instrument survives but the maker's research papers were destroyed?
tier_A_high_value_comparators.next_step: Map surviving engine, photographs, known test rulings, later William Stone records and printed publications while marking the destroyed-paper gap explicitly.

tier_B_hold_until_named_bridge: Kew microscope-slide collection: highly structured but primarily established in the 1930s; use only if a named nineteenth-century transferred subcollection is identified.

Zoological Survey of India aggregate slide/type holdings: institutional lineage reaches Asiatic Society/Indian Museum collections, but do not infer that current slide holdings are nineteenth-century without a named accession or type series.

Charité historical preparation tools and Virchow collections: important microscopy/pathology context, but promote only when a surviving microscopic preparation or explicit slide catalogue is identified.
Edinburgh Anatomical Museum records: strong nineteenth-century museum archive, but keep outside the slide-first layer until microscopic slide/preparation series are explicitly documented.
execution_order: Quekett/Oxford RMS first because existing project IDs already permit direct object closure with minimal new digitisation.
Tokyo second because the record-number sequence is bounded and could generate an independent institutional-history paper.
Cambridge Balfour next because slides, sectioning apparatus, historical documentation and publication form a rare integrated production chain.
Naples and La Plata next because existing catalogue/series work already supplies item-level anchors.
Coimbra and Würzburg then build the comparative teaching axis; both should be approached through inventories/catalogues before broad archival requests.
Manchester/Dundee then feed the commercial-maker crosswalk; use surviving labels to decide which trade catalogues deserve full extraction.
Haeckel is best treated as a bounded digital corpus harvest, not an open-ended biographical archive search.
Grayson remains a methodological control for archival asymmetry rather than a conventional provenance closure.
